clauses.clause: Share relevant information about a topic (C)
clauses.note: Students share information they learned about their selected sky pattern with a partner, drawing on their notes — the information is on-topic (relevant) and drawn from their research notes.

clauses.clause: Share accurate information about a topic (C)
clauses.note: Students use their research notes (pictures, labels, facts gathered across the unit) to share information, grounding their sharing in documented observations and thus supporting accuracy.

clauses.clause: Use a variety of communication modes to share information (C)
clauses.note: Students share information orally (Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face partner sharing, whole-group share-outs) and through physical gestures/motions representing sky patterns, and they write observations in their Sky Notebook — oral and written modes are present, plus gestural. However, the lesson's primary sharing vehicle is oral; the written mode (Sky Notebook) is an observation recording task rather than a sharing-with-an-audience act, and the gestures are a review activity rather than a communicative sharing mode. The variety is thin but present across at least two modes (oral sharing and written notebook entry).

verdicts.evidence: 'What are one or two pieces of information you learned about this pattern in the sky?' (Responses will vary, depending on chosen pattern.)
verdicts.rationale: The standard requires students to share relevant and accurate information through a variety of different modes (C — construction). In Work Time C, students share information about their selected sky pattern with partners using the Back-to-Back and Face-to-Face protocol: "What are one or two pieces of information you learned about this pattern in the sky?" Students use their research notes to share, supporting both relevance and accuracy. The "variety of different modes" clause is only partially met: students share orally with partners and the whole group, and they write observations in their Sky Notebook, but the written notebook entry is a recording task rather than a communicative sharing act directed at an audience, making the variety of modes thin. The gestural/body-motion activity (Work Time A) is a review exercise, not an information-sharing mode. Full alignment would require clearer use of multiple distinct communication modes (e.g., oral presentation plus a written or visual product shared with an audience).
verdicts.grounding_note: evidence quote found in lesson raw text
verdicts.standard_raw_text: Share relevant and accurate information through a variety of different modes. (C)

clauses.clause: Craft texts that engage readers (C — student produces/constructs a text)
clauses.note: Students independently write a Sky notebook entry (a constructed text), but the task is a structured observation recording exercise guided by a photograph and anchor charts, not a task with instructional intent focused on crafting engaging texts for a reader.

verdicts.evidence: Remind students to use the Prepositions anchor chart, Adjectives anchor chart, and the Sun, Moon, and Stars Word Wall as necessary.
verdicts.rationale: Students independently write a Sky notebook entry about the moon (Closing and Assessment A), and the lesson directs them to use the Adjectives anchor chart, Prepositions anchor chart, and Word Wall while writing — pointing toward use of descriptive words in a constructed text. However, the instructional intent of the writing task is to record observations from a photograph, not to deliberately craft an engaging text using descriptive language. The use of descriptive words is incidental scaffolding (anchor charts available as reference) rather than the lesson's targeted skill, and there is no explicit instruction or student practice focused on making the text engaging for a reader. Both clauses are therefore partially met: descriptive words are prompted but not the lesson's focus, and the student produces a text but not one aimed at engaging readers.
